questiontext.text: What does the blue rule (cut rule) for minimum spanning trees state?

answer.text: The minimum-weight edge crossing any cut belongs to some MST

feedback.text: Correct — color that edge blue (include it).

answer.text: The maximum-weight edge crossing any cut belongs to some MST

feedback.text: No — the blue rule includes the minimum crossing edge, not the maximum.

answer.text: The minimum-weight edge on any cycle belongs to some MST

feedback.text: That confuses the cut with the cycle; the cycle rule concerns the maximum edge on a cycle.

answer.text: Every edge crossing a cut belongs to the MST

feedback.text: Only the minimum crossing edge is guaranteed, not all of them.

generalfeedback.text: Blue rule: across any cut of the graph, the cheapest crossing edge is safe to include in an MST.

answer.text: The maximum-weight edge on any cycle can be excluded from some MST

feedback.text: Correct — color that edge red (exclude it).

answer.text: The minimum-weight edge on any cycle must be excluded

feedback.text: No — the red rule excludes the maximum edge of a cycle.

answer.text: The maximum-weight edge crossing any cut is excluded

feedback.text: That mixes up cut and cycle; the red rule is about cycles.

answer.text: Every edge on a cycle is excluded

feedback.text: Only the heaviest cycle edge is safe to exclude.

generalfeedback.text: Red rule: on any cycle, the heaviest edge is safe to drop from an MST.

questiontext.text: Why are the red and blue rules important in MST theory?

answer.text: They form a unifying correctness framework of which Kruskal, Prim, and Boruvka are instances

feedback.text: Correct — each classic MST algorithm is a particular strategy for applying these two rules.

answer.text: They only apply to directed graphs

feedback.text: MSTs and these rules are defined on undirected weighted graphs.

answer.text: They compute shortest paths, not spanning trees

feedback.text: They concern MSTs, not shortest paths.

answer.text: They replace the need for edge weights

feedback.text: The rules compare edge weights, so weights are essential.

generalfeedback.text: The red-blue rules prove that greedily including safe (blue) edges and excluding useless (red) edges yields an MST, unifying Kruskal, Prim, and Boruvka.

questiontext.text: In the red-blue method, what does coloring an edge blue mean?

answer.text: The edge is accepted into the MST

feedback.text: Correct — blue means included.

answer.text: The edge is rejected from the MST

feedback.text: That is red (excluded), not blue.

answer.text: The edge is temporarily ignored

feedback.text: Blue is a definite include decision, not a deferral.

answer.text: The edge forms a negative cycle

feedback.text: MST theory here is about weight, not negative cycles.

generalfeedback.text: Blue = include (safe edge via the cut rule); red = exclude (useless edge via the cycle rule).

questiontext.text: Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms can both be viewed as specific ways of applying the red-blue rules.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — they are instances of the same unifying framework.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Both are indeed instances of the red-blue rules.

questiontext.text: The cut rule (blue rule) tells you to include the maximum-weight edge crossing a cut.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — the cut rule includes the minimum-weight crossing edge.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — it is the minimum crossing edge that is safe to include.

questiontext.text: The blue rule is stated in terms of a partition of the vertices into two sets, called a ______ (one word, English term).

answer.text: cut

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: cut*

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about the red-blue rules are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: The blue (cut) rule includes the minimum edge crossing a cut

feedback.text: Yes — that safe edge belongs to some MST.

answer.text: The red (cycle) rule excludes the maximum edge on a cycle

feedback.text: Yes — the heaviest cycle edge is not needed.

answer.text: The blue rule includes the maximum crossing edge

feedback.text: No — it includes the minimum crossing edge.

answer.text: The rules compute all-pairs shortest paths

feedback.text: No — they build a minimum spanning tree.

generalfeedback.text: Blue rule: minimum edge across a cut is included; red rule: maximum edge on a cycle is excluded. Together they prove MST algorithms correct.
